clinicalPearls: Characterised by episodes of burning pain, marked redness and heat, most often affecting the feet and sometimes the hands
Symptoms are triggered or worsened by warmth, exercise and dependency, and are characteristically relieved by cooling and elevation of the affected part
Patients often seek relief by immersing the limbs in cold water, which can itself lead to maceration, ulceration and non-healing skin damage
The disorder is divided into primary (idiopathic or inherited) and secondary forms, the latter most importantly associated with myeloproliferative disease
Myeloproliferative-associated erythromelalgia, particularly with polycythaemia vera or essential thrombocythaemia (often JAK2-related), characteristically responds to low-dose aspirin
An inherited primary form is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the SCN9A gene encoding the Nav1.7 sodium channel, presenting early in life
A full blood count is essential in every patient to detect an underlying myeloproliferative disorder, which may precede an overt haematological diagnosis

Management combines cooling, elevation and avoidance of triggers with aspirin for myeloproliferative-associated disease and treatment of any underlying cause; primary neuropathic forms are often difficult to control
reference.pathophysiology: Erythromelalgia reflects a mismatch between skin perfusion and metabolic demand, with maldistribution of blood flow causing both increased superficial perfusion (redness and warmth) and paradoxical tissue hypoxia that generates burning pain. In myeloproliferative-associated disease, platelet-mediated microvascular occlusion and inflammation within the small vessels are thought to drive the symptoms, which is why antiplatelet therapy with aspirin is so effective. In the inherited primary form, gain-of-function mutations in the SCN9A gene increase the excitability of the Nav1.7 sodium channel in peripheral sensory and sympathetic neurons, lowering the threshold for pain and vasomotor dysregulation. Secondary erythromelalgia may also accompany drugs, connective tissue disease and neuropathies, reflecting varied vascular and neural mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral neuropathy, including small-fibre and diabetic neuropathy
Raynaud phenomenon and other vasospastic disorders
Cellulitis or other infective causes of a hot red limb
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count to detect polycythaemia vera or essential thrombocythaemia
JAK2 mutation analysis and haematology referral when a myeloproliferative cause is suspected
Genetic testing for SCN9A mutations in early-onset or familial disease
Screening for secondary causes including autoimmune, neuropathic and drug-related triggers
Assessment of skin for cold-immersion damage, maceration and secondary infection
Vascular and neurological assessment to exclude mimics such as ischaemia or neuropathy
redFlags: An underlying myeloproliferative disorder revealed by an abnormal blood count
Tissue damage, ulceration or infection from repeated cold-water immersion
Rapid onset or severe unremitting pain suggesting a secondary or ischaemic cause
Thrombotic or bleeding complications in myeloproliferative-associated disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with the cause: myeloproliferative-associated erythromelalgia often improves markedly with aspirin and treatment of the blood disorder, whereas primary and neuropathic forms tend to be chronic and refractory, and complications may arise from aggressive cooling behaviours.
pitfalls: Omitting a full blood count and missing an underlying myeloproliferative disorder that may respond to aspirin
Encouraging or overlooking harmful prolonged cold-water immersion that damages the skin
Attributing the hot red limb to cellulitis and giving unnecessary antibiotics
Failing to consider an inherited sodium-channel cause in early-onset or familial cases
references: British Journal of Haematology guidance on myeloproliferative neoplasms
management: Low-dose aspirin as first-line antiplatelet therapy, dramatically effective in myeloproliferative-associated disease
Refer to haematology to identify and treat any underlying polycythaemia vera or essential thrombocythaemia driving symptoms
For primary or neuropathic disease, neuropathic and sodium-channel-directed agents such as gabapentinoids, mexiletine or carbamazepine
Symptomatic relief by cooling and limb elevation, while counselling against prolonged cold-water immersion that causes maceration, ulceration and secondary infection
Advise avoidance of triggers including warmth, exertional overheating and limb dependency
Review and withdraw provoking drugs and treat identified secondary causes
SCN9A genetic testing and counselling in early-onset or familial disease
